column8: Where the case warrants alternative accounting treatment, switches (flags) should allow assets to be capitalized or expensed without rebuilding the model. A case that never requires such a treatment change satisfies this item by default.
column9: Switches allow the capitalize-versus-expense treatment to be changed where the case warrants it - or the case does not require such treatment changes.
column10: The case warrants capitalize-versus-expense analysis, but no switches exist and the change would require a rebuild.
column11: Where the case warrants alternative accounting treatment, do switches allow assets to be capitalized or expensed without a rebuild?
column12: Switches (flags) that toggle between capitalizing and expensing allow what-if analysis on accounting treatment without rebuilding the model. Where the case never raises such a question, the item is satisfied by default.
column14: Applies: cases where capitalize-versus-expense is a live question - R&D, software or development costs, leases, tooling, major maintenance, exploration, borrowing costs - or where the brief asks for an accounting-treatment sensitivity or a comparison of treatments. N/A: cases where the treatment of every cost is settled by the brief or by the nature of the spend ('R&D is x% of net revenue', 'machines are depreciated straight-line over n years'), so a switch would toggle between one permitted answer and one forbidden one. How to tell from the starting file: read the cost and capex rules on the instructions and assumptions tabs. If the treatment of every category is prescribed, mark N/A. If a treatment is left open, or the brief asks what the result would be under the alternative, apply.

column8: If the model was created to evaluate a business opportunity and later reuse (e.g., as an ongoing planning tool) is foreseeable, the design should support that reuse. If no reuse is foreseeable (i.e. ruled out in the instructions), the item is satisfied by default.
column9: Design supports both initial evaluation and foreseeable later reuse (e.g., as a planning tool) - or no ongoing reuse is foreseeable.
column10: Design suits only one-time evaluation despite a foreseeable need for ongoing reuse.
column11: Where the model is likely to be reused later (e.g., as an ongoing planning tool), does the build support that reuse?
column12: A one-time transaction model differs from a planning tool in refresh cadence, required flexibility, and output depth. Where later reuse is foreseeable, that must shape design choices today; where no reuse is foreseeable, the item is satisfied by default. This item assesses the flexibility of the build; whether the overall structure matches the deal-versus-planning intent is assessed separately under Structure.
column14: Applies: cases where the brief indicates the model will be refreshed, maintained or reused - budgeting, forecasting, FP&A, ongoing monitoring, a rolling plan, a tool to be handed to a client - or where reuse is the natural next step from the stated purpose. N/A: strictly one-off analyses where reuse is ruled out or clearly not contemplated - a one-time valuation answering a fixed question set from a static data pack. How to tell from the starting file: read the task framing at the top of the instructions tab. 'FP&A task', 'build an operating plan', 'monthly liquidity model' means apply. 'Valuation task - value the company from this data and answer these questions' means N/A.

column8: Assumptions and time periods must be updated (rolled forward, extended, or re-granularized) without manual rework.
column9: Assumptions and periods update easily; the model rolls forward without rework.
column10: Updating periods or rolling forward requires extensive manual rework.
column11: Can time periods and their assumptions be updated - rolled forward, extended, or re-granularized - without manual rework?
column12: Temporal flexibility means assumptions and time periods can be updated easily (e.g., rolling the model forward by a quarter, extending projections, or adjusting period granularity between monthly, quarterly, and annual) without manual rework. Date-driven logic should cascade from a single period-start cell. Critical for ongoing-use models.
column14: Applies: any case with a period timeline - forecasts, schedules, budgets, roll-forwards, amortization or coupon schedules - where extending the horizon, rolling the start date forward, or changing granularity (daily, monthly, quarterly, annual) is conceivable. N/A: cases with no time dimension - a single-point valuation, a snapshot allocation, a one-shot sizing calculation. How to tell from the starting file: look for a model duration, start date, forecast period or maturity on the assumptions tab. Where a 'model duration' or 'forecast period' input exists, apply, and expect the horizon and every period header to be driven from that cell rather than hardcoded or extended by hand. A brief stating that the model 'must remain correct for any combination of the inputs' makes this item central rather than optional.

column8: The model should be driver-based and formulaic so that changes to inputs or additions of new line items can be made quickly.
column9: The model is driver-based and formulaic; changes and additions are quick.
column10: The model relies on hardcoded values or rigid structures that require manual rework to update or extend.
column11: Is the model built in a flexible, dynamic way, so that changes or additions can be made quickly?
column12: A flexible, dynamic build (driver-based, formulaic, no hardcoded calcs) allows the model to respond quickly to changes and remain useful over time.

column8: Actuals (historical, fixed) and forecasts (editable, driver-based) should be clearly separated by labeling, formatting or a vertical divider so the transition point is obvious.
column9: Actuals and forecasts are clearly separated; the transition point is obvious.
column10: Actuals and forecasts look identical, are not labeled, and/or the transition point is unclear.
column11: Are actuals clearly separated from forecasts (different formatting/a vertical divider)?
column12: Clear separation between actuals (historical, fixed) and forecast (editable, driver-based) prevents the user from accidentally overwriting history and makes the transition point obvious.
column14: Applies: cases that supply historical or actual data alongside a forecast - opening or closing balances for a prior year, reported financials to be extended, a base period the model must continue from, actual-versus-budget columns. N/A in two distinct situations: cases that are entirely forward-looking with no historical period (a greenfield project, a new venture, a pure scenario build), AND cases that are entirely historical or static with no forecast at all (a table of reported figures, a comparable-company set). In both there is no transition point to mark. How to tell from the starting file: does the pack supply a closing balance sheet, prior-year actuals, or a base period the model must continue from? If yes, apply, and expect the boundary between the last actual and the first forecast column to be visible without reading formulas.

column8: Input cells must be visually marked (color, shading, border) so users immediately know where they can safely enter values.
column9: Input cells are clearly marked as safe-to-edit.
column10: Input cells are not distinguished from formula cells via formatting.
column11: Are input cells visually marked (color, shading, or border) so users know where to enter values?
column12: Input cells should be visually marked (color, shading, border) so users immediately know where they can safely enter values without destroying the model.

column8: Key input cells should use data validation to constrain entries to allowable ranges or types, warning the user when an entry falls outside the range deemed appropriate.
column9: Key input cells use data validation to constrain entries to sensible ranges, types, or lists, so an out-of-range entry is rejected or flagged at the point of entry.
column10: Input cells accept any entry; no data validation constrains values, types, or lists, even where an out-of-range entry would break the model silently.
column11: Do key input cells use data validation to constrain entries to allowable ranges or types?
column12: Data validation stops an implausible input at the point of entry rather than letting it propagate into the outputs, and a dropdown list also documents the permitted values for the next user. It is most valuable where a wrong entry is silent rather than obvious - a growth rate entered as 5 instead of 0.05, a scenario selector pointing at a case that does not exist, or a date outside the model's timeline.
column14: Applies: cases calling for user-operated controls - scenario or case selectors, toggles, switches, sensitivity inputs, or a dropdown-driven choice such as coupon frequency or day-count basis - and cases containing bounded inputs where a wrong entry would propagate silently instead of breaking visibly (rates that must lie between 0% and 100%, dates that must fall inside the model timeline, a text input that must match one of a listed set of values). N/A: cases that are a fixed computation from a supplied input set, with no cell a user is expected to change after delivery. How to tell from the starting file: does the brief ask for scenarios or sensitivities, state that the model must remain correct for other input combinations, or hand over an input whose permitted values are enumerated? If yes, apply. Borderline: a 'model duration', 'start date' or 'frequency' input is user-operable even where no scenarios are requested, so apply where such a cell exists.

column8: Number formats should be reasonable: no excess decimals, currency symbols where needed, thousands separators applied.
column9: Number formats are sensible and professional.
column10: Number formats are unreasonable (e.g., excess decimals, missing symbols or separators).
column11: Are chosen number formats reasonable?
column12: Reasonable number formats (no excess decimals, currency symbols where needed, thousands separators) make outputs readable and professional.

column8: Number formats must be consistent across the model for comparable values.
column9: Number formats are consistent for comparable values across the model (also consistent is the number of shown decimals for comparable values).
column10: Number formats vary inconsistently for comparable values.
column11: Are chosen number formats used consistently?
column12: Consistent number formats across the model avoid confusion and support quick visual scanning.

column8: Bright yellow highlighting used during model construction to flag TBD, placeholder, or work-in-progress items must be entirely removed from the final deliverable. This does not apply to yellow used intentionally in the delivered model for a defined purpose - for example conditional formatting on error-check rows, a documented convention for marking input cells, or flagging assumptions that require periodic review - provided such usage is to be explained in the model's glossary or conventions guide.
column9: No bright yellow cells signaling unfinished or placeholder work remain in the final product. Any yellow used intentionally for a documented, ongoing purpose (e.g., error-check conditional formatting, marked input cells, flagged review items) is explained in the glossary or conventions.
column10: Cells with bright yellow fill that appear to mark unfinished, placeholder, or TBD items remain in the delivered workbook, signaling incomplete work - or yellow is used for an ongoing purpose but is not documented in the glossary, making it indistinguishable from leftover WIP markers.
column11: Is the final product free of bright yellow highlighting signaling unfinished work, with any intentional use of yellow documented?
column12: Bright yellow is the standard highlight color for work-in-progress or TBD items during model construction, and any left in the delivered file signals incomplete work. Yellow used deliberately for a defined, ongoing purpose - error-check conditional formatting, marked input cells, flagged review items - is acceptable, but only where the glossary or conventions section documents that meaning; otherwise the reader cannot distinguish it from a leftover WIP marker.

column8: Hardcoded inputs must use blue font per industry-standard color coding.
column9: Hardcoded inputs consistently use blue font.
column10: Inputs do not use blue font.
column11: Is the font color of inputs blue?
column12: Blue font marks a cell as a hardcoded input that a user may safely change. Applied consistently, it lets an auditor see at a glance which numbers drive the model and which are derived from it.

column8: Formulas and calculations must use black font per industry-standard color coding.
column9: Formulas and calculations consistently use black font.
column10: Calculations do not use black font.
column11: Is the font color of calculations black?
column12: Black font marks a cell as a formula calculated on its own sheet. Together with blue inputs, it lets a reviewer distinguish derived values from entered ones without clicking into each cell.

column8: Cells linking to other sheets should use green font per industry-standard color coding.
column9: Cross-sheet links consistently use green font.
column10: Cross-sheet links do not use green font.
column11: Is the font color of calculation cells that are linked to other sheets green?
column12: Green font marks a formula that pulls its value from another sheet in the same workbook, so a reviewer can see immediately where a number crosses a sheet boundary and needs tracing elsewhere.
column14: Applies: any case whose scope implies more than one sheet - in practice nearly all - so that inputs, calculations and outputs sit on different tabs and cross-sheet links exist to be colored. N/A: only where the case genuinely implies a single-sheet deliverable, so no cross-sheet reference can exist and the item could only ever be passed vacuously. How to tell from the starting file: if the case pack itself separates instructions, assumptions, data and questions across tabs, or the brief demands several schedules, apply. Note: this item gates only the green cross-sheet-link convention. Blue font for hardcoded inputs, black font for calculations, and the requirement that whatever color scheme is used be applied consistently are separate checks that stay in force for every model and are not switched off with it.

column8: Cells containing external links (references to other workbooks) should use red font per industry-standard color coding. If the model contains no external links, this item is satisfied by default.
column9: External links consistently use red font - or no external links exist (satisfied by default).
column10: External links are present but do not use red font, making them indistinguishable from internal formulas or cross-sheet links.
column11: Is the font color of cells that are linked externally red?
column12: Red font marks a formula that references another workbook. Because external links break when the source file moves and hide dependencies (see 'No external links'), they must be visible on sight. A model with no external links satisfies this item by default.
column14: Applies: only where the case supplies data in a SEPARATE workbook, or explicitly permits or requires references to another file - a market-data extract, a supplied comparables workbook to be linked rather than copied, a group template fed from subsidiary files. N/A: self-contained case packs delivered as a single workbook - the normal situation - where external links should not exist at all and the color convention has nothing to describe. How to tell from the starting file: count the files handed over and read whether the brief permits or requires linking out. One file and no permission means N/A. Note: this item covers only the color convention where such links are legitimate. The requirement that a model contain no undisclosed external links to other workbooks is a separate danger check that stays in force for every model, so a build that links out anyway is still penalized there.

column8: The color-coding scheme (blue inputs, black formulas, green links, red external links) must be applied consistently throughout. Inconsistent color coding is worse than none.
column9: Color coding is applied consistently across the entire model. Cell purpose is immediately clear from color alone.
column10: Color coding is applied inconsistently, making cell types unreliable to identify by color.
column11: Is the industry-standard color coding used consistently?
column12: Color coding only works when applied consistently. Inconsistent color coding is worse than none, as it misleads the reader.

column8: Formatting (fonts, sizes, alignment, borders, section styling) should be consistent across all sheets. Compare across sheets, not just within a single sheet.
column9: The same font family, sizing, and styling are used consistently across all sheets for comparable content.
column10: Different sheets use different fonts, sizes, or styles for comparable content.
column11: Is formatting in general (especially font formatting) used consistently throughout the model?
column12: Consistent formatting overall (fonts, alignment, borders, section styling) is professional practice and supports efficient review.

column8: The number of additional colors used beyond the industry-standard blue/black/green/red convention should be limited to a small, cohesive palette rather than a wide variety of different colors.
column9: Only a limited number of additional colors (or none) are used as font color (beyond the industry-standard blue/black/green/red convention), background color, and tab color, forming a cohesive palette rather than a rainbow of different hues.
column10: A wide variety of different colors is used throughout the model, creating an unprofessional, overly colorful appearance.
column11: Is the number of additional colors (beyond industry-standard coding) limited to a small, cohesive palette?
column12: Limiting the additional color palette keeps the model professional and ensures the intentional industry-standard color coding remains the dominant visual signal. Too many colors distract and overwhelm the reader.

column3: No colors that mimic standard coding
column8: Additional colors must not closely resemble the standard blue/black/green/red coding, which would mislead the reader about cell types.
column9: No additional colors closely resemble the blue, black, green or red used in the industry-standard color-coding convention.
column10: Colors are used that closely resemble the industry-standard color coding, making it unreliable to identify cell types by color.
column11: Are additional colors kept clearly distinct from the industry-standard blue/black/green/red coding?
column12: If additional colors resemble the standard coding colors, readers can no longer reliably identify inputs, formulas, cross-sheet links, and external links by color alone, undermining the primary purpose of the convention.

column8: The number of cells and elements carrying additional color formatting (beyond cells subject to the industry-standard color coding) should be limited to avoid visual clutter and distraction from the intentional coding scheme.
column9: Only a limited number of cells and elements beyond those subject to industry-standard color coding carry additional color formatting (font, background, or tab color).
column10: Too many cells or elements are colored beyond the standard coding scheme, creating visual clutter that distracts from the intentional color-coding.
column11: Are additional color-formatted cells and elements (beyond industry-standard coding) kept to a minimum?
column12: Even with an appropriate palette, applying color to too many cells or elements dilutes the visual signal of the industry-standard coding and makes the model look unprofessional.

column8: Conditional formatting should be limited to error-check rows, data-validation indicators, and threshold alerts, and must not override the blue/black/green/red color-coding convention.
column9: Conditional formatting is limited and does not conflict with the color-coding scheme.
column10: Conditional formatting overrides color coding, making cell types unreliable to identify by color.
column11: Is conditional formatting used sparingly, and not conflicting with the standard color-coding scheme?
column12: Overuse of conditional formatting can override the blue/black/green/red color-coding convention and make cell colors unreliable for distinguishing inputs from formulas. Where used, it should be limited - primarily to error-check rows, data-validation indicators, and threshold alerts.

column8: Borders should be used sparingly to partition sections and separate key areas of the model. Excessive border usage creates a cluttered, unprofessional look.
column9: Borders are used sparingly to partition sections; the model has a clean, uncluttered appearance.
column10: Excessive borders are applied throughout the model, creating a cluttered and unprofessional look.
column11: Are borders used sparingly to partition sections without excessive use?
column12: Borders should serve a structural purpose - partitioning information into logical sections. Overuse clutters the visual layout, makes sections harder to distinguish rather than easier, and looks unprofessional.

column8: Shading (cell fill color) should be used consistently to highlight headers and titles only, making them visually distinct from data rows.
column9: Shading is applied consistently to headers and titles only, making headings visually distinct from data rows in a professional manner.
column10: Shading is applied excessively across many rows or sections, or headings are not visually distinct from data rows.
column11: Is shading used consistently and only for headers and titles, following professional conventions?
column12: Coloring and shading of subtitles, headers, and titles should be consistent. Shading applied beyond headers dilutes their visual prominence and creates clutter.

column8: Totals and subtotals should be bolded or otherwise visually distinguished from regular line items.
column9: Totals and subtotals are visually distinguished (e.g., bolded, underlined).
column10: Totals and subtotals are indistinguishable from regular line items.
column11: Are totals and subtotals bolded or otherwise visually distinguished from regular line items?
column12: Totals and subtotals should be visible at first glance and therefore visually distinct from the regular line items feeding them.

column8: Every sheet should use the same zoom level across the entire workbook (commonly 75%, 80%, or 100%) so the model does not jump in scale when navigating between tabs.
column9: All sheets use the same zoom level (commonly 100%, 80%, or 75%), providing a consistent viewing experience.
column10: Zoom levels vary across sheets, creating an inconsistent and unprofessional viewing experience.
column11: Is a consistent zoom level (100%, 80%, or 75%) applied across all sheets?
column12: Inconsistent zoom levels across tabs disrupt the reader's experience and signal a lack of attention to detail. A uniform zoom (typically 100%, 80%, or 75%) across all sheets is professional practice.

column3: Active cell reset to A1 on all sheets
column8: The cursor should be parked at cell A1 (or the sheet's designated home cell) on every sheet before delivery, so that each tab opens at its intended starting position.
column9: The cursor is parked at A1, or at the sheet's designated home cell; each tab opens at its intended starting position.
column10: The cursor is left mid-sheet on one or more tabs, causing sheets to open at unexpected positions.
column11: Is the cursor parked at cell A1 (or the sheet's designated home cell) on every sheet?
column12: Parking the cursor at A1 before delivery ensures the reader sees the top-left starting position of each sheet on opening. A cursor left mid-sheet is a common oversight that signals incomplete preparation.

column8: Text values should be left-aligned, with one standard exception: column headers above numeric columns (e.g., period labels such as 'FY2024A') may be right-aligned or centered so they align with the values beneath them.
column9: Body text and row labels are left-aligned; column headers over numeric columns may instead be right- or center-aligned.
column10: Text alignment is inconsistent or arbitrary (e.g., row labels right-aligned).
column11: Are all text values left-aligned inside their cells?
column12: Left-aligned text is the Excel default and the industry norm; row labels that drift to other alignments make a column of labels harder to scan. Column headers sitting above numeric columns are the standard exception and may be right-aligned or centered so they sit over their values.

column8: Numerical values should be right-aligned within their cells.
column9: Numerical values are right-aligned.
column10: Numerical values are not consistently right-aligned.
column11: Are all numerical values right-aligned inside their cells?
column12: Right-aligned numbers line up on their digits, so magnitudes can be compared down a column at a glance. It is both the Excel default for numeric values and the industry norm.

column8: Negative values should be displayed in parentheses, not with a minus sign, per finance convention.
column9: Negative values use parentheses, e.g., (123).
column10: Negative values use a minus sign, e.g., -123.
column11: Are negative values displayed with parentheses format instead of -?
column12: Finance convention shows negatives in parentheses rather than with a minus sign, because parentheses are easier to spot when scanning a column of figures. The convention should be applied through number formatting so it holds everywhere the value appears.

column8: Zero values should be displayed as dashes (-) rather than '0' per finance convention.
column9: Zero values display as dashes.
column10: Zero values display as '0'.
column11: Are numerical values that are zero displayed as dashes instead of 0?
column12: Finance convention displays zero as a dash rather than '0', which keeps a grid of figures readable and makes genuinely populated cells stand out. This is a display convention only - the underlying value remains zero.

column8: Monetary and other (large) quantity values should be formatted with a thousands separator. Values that conventionally carry none - years (2024, not 2,024), percentages, valuation multiples (e.g., 7.5x), and per-unit figures - are excluded.
column9: Thousands separators are applied to monetary and quantity values; years, percentages, multiples, and per-unit figures correctly carry none.
column10: Large monetary/quantity values lack thousands separators, or separators are wrongly applied (e.g., years shown as 2,024).
column11: Are monetary and quantity values formatted with a thousands separator, with years, percentages, multiples, and per-unit figures correctly excluded?
column12: Thousands separators make large figures readable at a glance and are standard practice. Values that conventionally carry none - years (2024, not 2,024), percentages, valuation multiples, and per-unit figures - must be excluded, since a separator on a year is an immediate signal of careless formatting.

column8: The currency used in the model must be clearly stated as a unit, and stated per block or column, especially in cases where FX is involved.
column9: The currency is clearly stated as a unit, including for each block or column.
column10: The currency is not stated, leaving values ambiguous.
column11: Is the currency clearly stated as a unit inside the model?
column12: Currency is a unit like any other and should be stated wherever values are presented - in the block or column header, not only on a cover sheet. This becomes critical wherever FX is involved: without a stated currency per block, a reader cannot tell whether a figure has already been translated, and adding two currencies together is a silent and expensive error.
column14: Applies: any case containing monetary values - nearly all - and with particular force where more than one currency appears or any FX translation is required, in which case the currency must be stated per block or per column and the rate used made explicit. N/A: only cases with no monetary figures anywhere - a pure volume, headcount, capacity, utilization, day-count or timing model. How to tell from the starting file: scan the assumptions tab and the answer tab for currency units or unit tags such as [$] or [EURm]. An FX table, or a mix of currency tags, means apply and grade strictly. A case whose answers are all in days, units or percentages means N/A.

column8: Column widths must be sufficient to display all values without truncation or '###'.
column9: All values display fully; no truncation or '###'.
column10: Some columns truncate values or show '###'.
column11: Are all column widths sufficient to display values without truncation or displaying '###'?
column12: Truncated values and '###' make a model unreadable and can hide the very figure the reader is looking for. Column widths must accommodate the values displayed.

column8: Column widths should not be excessive.
column9: Columns are no wider than their content requires; several full-width columns fit on screen at once, and long text is wrapped rather than accommodated by widening the column.
column10: The model contains excessively wide columns (rule of thumb: wider than roughly 75-80 characters at the default font), or long text is left unwrapped.
column11: Are column widths kept reasonable, with long text wrapped rather than accommodated by very wide columns?
column12: Excessively wide columns push content off-screen and force horizontal scrolling to read a single row. Where a long text entry is needed, wrapping the text is preferable to widening the column.

column8: Calculation columns on a sheet should share a consistent width. Header/text/unit columns may be wider.
column9: Calculation columns share a consistent width.
column10: Calculation column widths vary inconsistently.
column11: Are column widths used consistently, with calculation columns on the same sheet sharing one width and header/text columns allowed to be wider?
column12: Calculation columns of equal width keep the timeline visually even, so figures line up down the sheet and a resized column stands out immediately as an anomaly. Header, label, and unit columns are the standard exception and may be wider, since they carry text rather than periods.

column8: Row heights should be consistent within each tab.
column9: Row heights are consistent within each tab - Header rows may be higher.
column10: Row heights vary within a tab (exception: header rows).
column11: Are all row heights consistent within each tab?
column12: Consistent row heights keep a sheet visually even and make it obvious when a row has been resized to accommodate or conceal something unusual. Header rows may be taller, as they often carry wrapped labels.

column8: Row heights should not be excessive.
column9: Row heights are reasonable - by default, rows should be only one line high. While rows higher than one line are acceptable, they should be used sparingly.
column10: The model contains excessively tall rows (rule of thumb: taller than roughly 60 points).
column11: Are row heights kept reasonable?
column12: Excessively tall rows waste screen space and reduce the number of line items visible at once. Rows should be a single line high by default; taller rows are acceptable but should be used sparingly.

column8: Merged cells break Excel's grid logic (broken formulas, sorting failures, reference errors). Use Center Across Selection instead to preserve grid integrity.
column9: No merged cells; Center Across Selection is used where needed.
column10: Merged cells are present. (Merged cells on the Instructions Tab are allowed)
column11: Are merged cells avoided, with Center Across Selection used where centering across columns is needed?
column12: Merging cells in financial models breaks Excel's grid logic, causing broken formulas, sorting failures, and reference errors. To achieve the exact same clean, centered look without compromising functionality, Center Across Selection should be used instead of merging cells.

column8: Print areas should be defined on each tab so that only relevant content is included when the sheet is printed or exported to PDF.
column9: Print areas are defined on each tab, ensuring only relevant content prints.
column10: Print areas are not defined; printing captures empty space, extraneous content, or misses relevant content.
column11: Are print areas defined on each tab so only relevant content prints?
column12: Without defined print areas, printing or PDF export may include empty cells, scratch areas, or cut off relevant content. Setting print areas is a basic preparation step for any deliverable model.
column14: Applies: cases whose deliverable is meant to be read away from Excel - a board or committee pack, an investment memo, a client-facing summary, an exhibit, or any brief asking for a printable or PDF output. Where it applies, judge it on the sheets a reader would actually print (cover, summary, statements, outputs), not on every tab of the workbook. N/A: cases whose deliverable is the working file itself - an answer tab to be filled in, a computational schedule, or any build whose calculation sheets run to dozens or hundreds of period columns, where a print area on the model tabs carries no quality signal and would not be set by a competent modeler. How to tell from the starting file: look for any instruction to present, print, export, circulate or PDF something outside the workbook or the existence of a summary (rather the ask for it). If the brief only asks for a model and a set of answers, mark N/A.

column8: Page breaks should be configured so that each tab prints legibly as PDF or hard copy without splitting tables, sections, or key content awkwardly across pages.
column9: Page breaks are set so that tabs print legibly without splitting tables or sections across pages.
column10: Page breaks are not set or are poorly placed; tables or sections split awkwardly across pages when printed.
column11: Are page breaks configured so tabs print legibly without awkward content splits?
column12: Poor page breaks split tables or sections mid-way, making printed or PDF output difficult to read. Properly configured page breaks ensure the model is share-ready as hard copy or PDF.
column14: Applies: cases whose deliverable is meant to be read away from Excel - a board or committee pack, an investment memo, a client-facing summary, an exhibit, or any brief asking for a printable or PDF output. Where it applies, judge it on the sheets a reader would actually print (cover, summary, statements, outputs), not on every tab of the workbook. N/A: cases whose deliverable is the working file itself - an answer tab to be filled in, a computational schedule, or any build whose calculation sheets run to dozens or hundreds of period columns, where a print area on the model tabs carries no quality signal and would not be set by a competent modeler. How to tell from the starting file: look for any instruction to present, print, export, circulate or PDF something outside the workbook or the existence of a summary (rather the ask for it). If the brief only asks for a model and a set of answers, mark N/A.

column8: The workbook should be saved in a standard Excel format: .xlsx, or .xlsm where VBA/macros are present.
column9: The workbook is saved as .xlsx (.xlsm when VBA/Macros are present).
column10: The workbook is saved in a legacy or non-standard format (e.g., .xls, .csv, or an export from another spreadsheet application).
column11: Is the workbook saved in a standard Excel format (.xlsx, or .xlsm where macros are present)?
column12: Modern Excel formats are the industry norm: .xlsx for standard workbooks, .xlsm where macros are required. Legacy formats such as .xls impose row and feature limits and signal an out-of-date build.

column8: The model should avoid non-standard, uncommon formulas (e.g., FILTERXML, WEBSERVICE, Recursive LAMBDA) that are atypical in financial modeling.
column9: Only standard financial-modeling formulas are used.
column10: Uncommon or non-standard formulas (e.g., FILTERXML, WEBSERVICE, recursive LAMBDA) are present where standard alternatives exist.
column11: Does the model avoid any non-standard formula usage (like FILTERXML)?
column12: Financial modeling relies on a well-known formula set (SUM, IF, INDEX/MATCH, XLOOKUP, SUMIFS, SUMPRODUCT, MIN/MAX, ROUND, and similar). Non-standard formulas such as FILTERXML, WEBSERVICE, or recursive LAMBDA reduce portability across Excel versions, confuse reviewers unfamiliar with them, and are a common pattern in AI-generated models. If an uncommon formula is used, there should be a clear justification and a comment explaining its purpose.

column8: Modern functions should be preferred where they improve robustness or readability and where backward compatibility is not a constraint: XLOOKUP over VLOOKUP, IFS or SWITCH over deeply nested IFs, and LET for readable intermediate variables. INDEX/XMATCH remains a fully acceptable professional standard and is not penalized. Unless the case context states otherwise, assume the client uses a current version of Excel; where an older version must be supported, the legacy equivalents are acceptable, and the trade-off should be documented.
column9: Modern functions (XLOOKUP, XMATCH, IFS, SWITCH, LET) are used where they improve robustness and readability - or a legacy equivalent is used for a documented compatibility or performance reason, for example INDEX/XMATCH or nested IFs in a very large model, where they compute more efficiently than IFS or SWITCH (in that case efficiency > auditability).
column10: Fragile legacy constructs are used where a modern equivalent is clearly preferable and no compatibility or performance reason is given - most commonly VLOOKUP with a hardcoded column index, or IFs nested many levels deep.
column11: Does the model use modern functions where they are preferable (e.g., XLOOKUP instead of VLOOKUP), or document why a legacy equivalent was chosen?
column12: Modern replacements (XLOOKUP for VLOOKUP, IFS/SWITCH for nested IFs, LET for readability) are generally more robust and easier to read, and they avoid the fragility of a hardcoded column index. They are not universally better: INDEX/XMATCH is a long-standing professional standard that remains fully acceptable, and in very large models nested IF can compute more efficiently than IFS or SWITCH, so a documented performance-driven choice is legitimate. Note that XLOOKUP, XMATCH, LET, and LAMBDA require Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021+; where an older version must be supported, the legacy equivalents are acceptable.

column8: Volatile functions (INDIRECT, OFFSET, TODAY, NOW, RAND, RANDBETWEEN, INFO, CELL) recalculate on every change and should be avoided where possible.
column9: Volatile functions are avoided except where clearly justified (e.g., date-stamping).
column10: Volatile functions are present where avoidable.
column11: Does the model avoid the usage of volatile functions (i.e. INDIRECT and OFFSET)?
column12: Volatile functions (INDIRECT, OFFSET, TODAY, NOW, RAND, RANDBETWEEN, INFO, CELL) recalc on every change and slow the model down. Use INDEX as a non-volatile alternative to OFFSET, and static date values instead of TODAY/NOW. It is industry practice to avoid them.

column8: Formulas must reference assumption cells rather than embedding constants (e.g., =B5*0.21). The only accepted exceptions are purely mathematical constants (12 months, 365 days, 100 for percentage conversion) and technical remnants that are not true inputs.
column9: Formulas reference assumption cells; no inputs are buried as constants inside formulas.
column10: Formulas contain hardcoded numbers (e.g., =B5*0.21) that should be assumption references.
column11: Are formulas free of hardcoded numbers that should be assumption references?
column12: Hardcoded numbers inside formulas (e.g., =B5*0.21) are invisible to the reader and make the model inflexible. It is standard practice to reference assumption cells instead. Accepted exceptions are purely mathematical constants (e.g., 12 for months in a year, 365 for days, 100 for percentage conversion) and technical remnants that are not actual inputs.

column8: Formulas should be simple, readable, and broken into logical steps using helper columns, helper rows, or LET. As a practical guideline, a formula nesting more than about three functions deep ('3-clause rule') should be split. Some complexity is acceptable where splitting would bloat the model structure.
column9: Complex logic is broken into steps via helper rows/columns or LET. No formula nests more than about ~three functions deep without justification.
column10: Monolithic mega-formulas obscure logic. No helper columns when clearly needed. Difficult to understand or debug.
column11: Are formulas kept simple, readable, and broken into logical steps, with any remaining complexity justified by keeping the model structure lean?
column12: Short formulas broken into steps are auditable and maintainable; long mega-formulas are a common source of hidden errors, because the reviewer cannot see the intermediate results that would reveal a mistake. A practical guideline is to split any formula nesting more than about three functions deep ('3-clause rule'). Some complexity is defensible where splitting would add so many helper rows that the model becomes harder to follow overall - the two considerations have to be balanced.

column8: Formulas across a row (the timeline) and across similar blocks should be identical so that copy-paste works and exceptions are immediately obvious.
column9: Formulas are consistent across the timeline and across similar blocks.
column10: Formulas vary unexpectedly across a row or between comparable blocks.
column11: Are formulas consistent across formula blocks and across the model timeline?
column12: Formulas across a row (across the timeline) and across comparable blocks should be identical, so a formula can be copied along the timeline safely and any genuine exception stands out immediately. A single edited cell mid-row is one of the most common silent errors in financial models, because nothing about the output looks wrong.

column8: Where formulas must be inconsistent (e.g., the first period of a roll-forward), the cells should be visually flagged (distinctive fill, exception-marker column, cell comment, or error-check flag) so reviewers know the break is intentional.
column9: Intentional formula breaks are clearly flagged visually.
column10: Formula inconsistencies are unmarked, leaving reviewers unable to distinguish intentional exceptions from errors.
column11: Are inconsistent formulas marked clearly and visually?
column12: Where formulas must be inconsistent (e.g., the first period of a roll-forward), the cells should be marked visually so reviewers and readers know the break is intentional. Common techniques include a distinctive fill color, a dedicated exception-marker column, a cell comment, or flagging the row on the error-check sheet. The method matters less than making the inconsistency impossible to miss.

column8: Absolute, relative, and mixed references ($) must be anchored correctly. Incorrect anchoring silently pulls wrong data when formulas are copied, without producing a visible Excel error.
column9: References are anchored correctly; copied formulas pull the intended cells.
column10: References are mis-anchored; copying formulas silently pulls wrong data.
column11: Are absolute, relative, and mixed cell references ($ signs) used correctly in formulas?
column12: Incorrect anchoring is one of the most common formula errors, especially when formulas are copied across rows or down columns. A misplaced or missing $ sign can silently pull the wrong data without producing a visible Excel error - making it one of the hardest bugs to catch. Always verify that absolute references lock to the intended assumption cell, that relative references shift correctly when dragged across the timeline, and that mixed references (e.g., $B5 vs. B$5) anchor the correct axis for the copy direction.

column8: Anchoring conventions ($) should be applied consistently across comparable formulas/blocks.
column9: Anchoring is consistent across comparable formulas/blocks.
column10: Anchoring conventions are inconsistent across comparable formulas or blocks.
column11: Are absolute, relative, and mixed cell references ($ signs) used consistently in formulas?
column12: Anchoring conventions should be uniform across comparable formulas so that a reviewer can trust the pattern rather than auditing every cell individually. If one revenue-line formula uses $B$3 to anchor a growth rate while an identical cost-line formula uses B$3 or B3 for the same type of reference, the inconsistency forces cell-by-cell checking and increases the risk that a future copy-paste silently breaks the logic. Consistent anchoring across similar formula blocks is what makes a model safely extensible.

column8: Whole-column/row references (e.g., SUM(A:A)) force Excel to evaluate up to a million rows per formula. Use defined ranges, TrimRef (e.g., A:.A), table columns, or names instead.
column9: Defined or structured ranges are used; no whole-column/row references.
column10: Whole-column/row references (e.g., SUM(A:A)) are present.
column11: Are full-column / whole-row references (e.g. SUM(A:A)) avoided?
column12: Whole-column references force Excel to evaluate up to a million rows per formula, bloating recalc time and risking accidental inclusion of stray data below the intended range. Use explicitly bounded ranges (e.g., A2:A500), structured table column references, or defined names instead.

column8: Outputs should pass a directional sense check against intuition, industry benchmarks, comparable companies or transactions, or third-party estimates. The metrics to check depend on the model type - growth and margins for an operating model, IRR and money multiple for a transaction model, debt service cover for project finance, payback and NPV for a capex case, implied multiples for a valuation. The sense check is part of the model, not a separate exercise.
column9: The model includes an explicit sense-check section comparing its key outputs to benchmarks, comparables, or third-party estimates, using metrics appropriate to the model type.
column10: Outputs are implausible or inconsistent with benchmarks - or no sense check is present.
column11: Do the results make sense directionally, and does the model include an explicit sense check against benchmarks or comparables?
column12: A directional sense check - do the outputs match intuition, industry benchmarks, or external estimates? - is one of the most effective validation steps available and catches many errors that formula-level review misses. Which metrics to cross-reference depends on the model type: revenue growth and margins, returns such as ROIC/ROE/IRR, leverage and cover ratios, and implied valuation multiples against comparables.

column8: The model should include a key-ratios section computing the output metrics relevant to its purpose - for example margins, returns, leverage and cover ratios, growth rates, valuation multiples, or transaction returns.
column9: A dedicated section computes the key ratios and output metrics relevant to the model's purpose.
column10: No key-ratios or output metrics section.
column11: Does the model include a section calculating the key ratios and output values relevant to its purpose?
column12: A key-ratios and outputs section translates the model into the metrics its audience actually uses to make a decision. Which ratios matter depends on the model type - margins and growth for an operating plan, returns and leverage for a transaction model, cover ratios for a financing case.

column8: A summary should display results across all scenarios/cases in one place. A model that deliberately runs a single case satisfies this item by default.
column9: A summary displays results across all cases in one view - or the model deliberately runs a single case.
column10: No cross-case summary; results are buried in separate sheets.
column11: Does the model include a summary displaying results for all cases (or does it deliberately run a single case)?
column12: A summary displaying results across all cases side by side is what most readers will actually look at, and it is the only place the sensitivity of the answer to the case becomes visible. Without it, the model's insights stay buried across separate sheets.
column14: Applies: cases asking for more than one case, scenario, sensitivity or variant - base, upside and downside, 'what if X', a sensitivity table, two valuation methods to be compared side by side, or a switch that changes the whole run. N/A: cases that deliberately run one set of assumptions, where the brief neither asks for nor implies alternatives. How to tell from the starting file: search the instructions and questions tabs for the words scenario, case, sensitivity, upside or downside, or for a question asking for the result under changed assumptions. If every question resolves to one set of inputs, mark N/A. Borderline: a valuation reporting outputs at several statistics of one data set (25th percentile, median, mean, 75th percentile), or a model reporting the same result at several dates, is ONE run with several outputs rather than several scenarios - mark N/A, since presenting those outputs together is graded as part of the key-outputs requirement instead.

column8: The summary page should update automatically when inputs change; manual summaries go stale.
column9: The summary updates automatically with any input change.
column10: Summary values are hardcoded or copy-pasted rather than formula-linked; changing an input does not propagate to the summary.
column11: Has the summary page been automated so that it updates automatically when the output values change?
column12: Automation means the summary updates live with any input change, so the reader always sees current numbers. Manual summaries go stale the moment an input changes and are a frequent source of presentation errors. An automated summary ensures the cover/outputs reflect current model state.

column8: The file should be free of hidden or very hidden sheets. Any legitimate hidden sheet must be disclosed.
column9: No hidden or very hidden sheets, or any present are disclosed and justified.
column10: Undisclosed hidden or very hidden sheets are present.
column11: Is the file free of undisclosed hidden or very hidden sheets?
column12: Hidden sheets can hold important logic, sensitive data, or values the reader is unaware of, and 'very hidden' sheets do not even appear in the unhide dialog. Everything should be unhidden during review, and any sheet that legitimately stays hidden should be disclosed.

column8: The file should be free of hidden rows or columns. Use grouping instead of hiding.
column9: No hidden rows or columns; grouping is used where collapsing is needed.
column10: Hidden rows or columns are present.
column11: Is the file free of hidden rows and columns, with grouping used where collapsing is needed?
column12: Hidden rows and columns often contain calculations or inputs that the reader never sees, and a value can be hidden with no visual cue that anything is missing. Everything should be unhidden during review. Best practice is to avoid hiding altogether and use grouping instead, which collapses detail while leaving the outline markers visible.

column8: No content should be concealed by formatting - in particular white font on a white background, or a number format that renders a populated cell blank.
column9: No content is concealed by white-on-white formatting or by a blanking number format.
column10: Content is concealed via white-on-white formatting or a number format that hides the value.
column11: Is the model free of content concealed by white-on-white formatting or blanking number formats?
column12: White font on a white background is a common way to conceal content, as is a custom number format such as ';;;' that renders a cell blank. Neither belongs in a delivered model - nothing should be hidden from the reader.

column8: The file should be free of external links to other workbooks (unless the case context requires them), as they can break when the linked file moves, cause #REF! errors, and hide dependencies.
column9: No external links (unless required by the case context/stated in the instructions); the file is self-contained.
column10: External links to other workbooks are present.
column11: Is the file free of external links to other workbooks?
column12: External links (to other workbooks) can break when the linked file moves, cause #REF errors, and hide dependencies. Ideally, remove or replace with internal links.

column8: Any macros or VBA code must be disclosed, reviewed, and justified. Macros add complexity, security risk, and maintenance burden and should therefore be avoided.
column9: No macros/VBA, or any present are disclosed, reviewed, and justified.
column10: Undisclosed or unjustified macros/VBA are present.
column11: Is the file free of macros/VBA - or is any VBA present disclosed, reviewed, and justified?
column12: Macros and VBA introduce complexity, security concerns, and maintenance burden, and can make the model unusable for a client whose IT policy blocks macro-enabled files. Their presence should be known, reviewed, and justified.
column14: Applies: cases where the brief calls for, or plausibly warrants, macro or VBA automation - a custom user interface the client is meant to operate by button, batch operations across files or folders, a scripted iterative optimization loop, event-driven behavior, or a connection to an external system. Where the item applies, grade whether any code present is disclosed in visible documentation, reviewed and justified; a macro-free solution to such a case is a full pass, since native Excel is preferred wherever it will do the job. N/A: cases fully solvable with native formulas, tables, data validation, conditional formatting, Power Query, Goal Seek and iterative calculation, so macros have no legitimate role in the first place - effectively every standard financial-modeling case in this set. Mark N/A as well where the submission is produced by a system that cannot write macros into a workbook at all, since the item can then only ever be passed vacuously. How to tell from the starting file: take each required deliverable in turn and ask whether it is impossible without code. If none is, mark N/A. This is a scoping judgment about whether automation has a legitimate role in the CASE, not about what the submitted workbook happens to contain.

column8: Where VBA is present, evaluate whether it could be replaced by native Excel tools (e.g., array formulas instead of loops, data validation instead of custom dialogs). A file without VBA satisfies this item by default.
column9: No VBA is present, or any VBA is genuinely necessary and not replaceable by native tools.
column10: VBA is present and duplicates what native Excel tools could achieve.
column11: Where VBA is present, is it genuinely necessary rather than replaceable by native Excel functionality?
column12: A large share of VBA in financial models substitutes for native Excel functionality - loops where SUMIFS or a formula would do, custom dialogs where data validation would do, button-driven copy-paste where a scenario switch would do. Each such case adds a dependency and a maintenance burden for no gain, so challenge whether the code is genuinely necessary before accepting it.
column14: Applies: only where the case genuinely demands automation that native Excel cannot deliver - a custom user interface, batch operations across files or folders, a scripted iterative optimization loop, a connection to an external system, or event-driven behavior - so that the question 'could this have been done without code?' has real content. N/A: cases solvable end to end with native formulas, tables, data validation, conditional formatting, Power Query, Goal Seek and iterative calculation - effectively every standard financial-modeling case in this set. Mark N/A as well where the submission is produced by a system that cannot write macros into a workbook at all, since no code can then exist to assess. How to tell from the starting file: take each required deliverable in turn and ask whether it is impossible using native features. If none is, mark N/A. This is a scoping judgment about whether automation has a legitimate role in the CASE, not about what the submitted workbook happens to contain. Note: this item asks only whether code, if present, was NECESSARY - whether the same result was reachable with native features. Whether that code was disclosed and justified is a separate question and is not graded here.

column8: A single sign convention (e.g., costs negative, revenues positive) must be applied consistently across the entire model, with particular attention to EBITDA add-backs, cash flow statement conventions, and income statement expense treatment.
column9: Sign conventions are consistent across the model.
column10: The same economic item carries different signs depending on where it appears (e.g., D&A is negative on the income statement but also negative in the EBITDA reconciliation instead of being added back as positive).
column11: Are +/- signs used consistently across the model? (cost normally negative in parentheses, revenues positive, …)
column12: Consistent sign conventions (costs negative, revenues positive, cash outflows negative) across the model make it faster to review and understand. Pay particular attention to EBITDA reconciliation (D&A as positive add-back), the cash flow statement (investing/financing outflows as negative), and the income statement (expenses must be treated consistently - either all positive with subtraction operators, or all negative with SUM). Inconsistent sign conventions are a leading cause of double-counting and missed items in consolidations.

column8: The model should still work when key assumptions are changed substantially (e.g., useful life tripled, valuation date shifted 12 months, revenue halved). Stress-testing exposes hidden breaks, balance sheet imbalances, divide-by-zero errors, and broken roll-forwards.
column9: The model produces sensible results under stress scenarios (e.g., revenue halved, useful life tripled, valuation date shifted). No Excel errors or balance-sheet imbalances emerge.
column10: Under stress, the model breaks, produces balance sheet imbalances, throws Excel errors, or generates nonsensical results (e.g., negative useful life, or negative shares outstanding).
column11: Does the model still work reliably if some of the key assumptions are changed substantially (e.g. useful life, valuation date, key operating assumptions)?
column12: Stress-testing with extreme-but-plausible inputs (e.g., useful life 3x, valuation date shifted 12 months, revenue halved) exposes hidden formula breaks, balance sheet imbalances, divide-by-zero errors, negative cash that the revolver is not catching, and broken roll-forwards. If the model falls over or produces nonsense under stress, the build is not robust.

column8: The workbook should be delivered with calculation set to automatic - and, where intentional circularity requires it, with iterative calculation enabled and that requirement stated. Manual calculation mode means displayed values may not reflect the inputs currently shown.
column9: Calculation is set to automatic, with iterative calculation enabled and documented where the model uses intentional circularity.
column10: The workbook is saved in manual calculation mode without disclosure, so displayed values may be stale - or iterative calculation is required but not enabled.
column11: Is the workbook set to automatic calculation (with iterative calculation enabled where circularity requires it)?
column12: A workbook saved in manual calculation mode displays whatever was last computed, which may bear no relation to the inputs currently shown: a reader can change an assumption and see nothing move. Manual mode is occasionally used deliberately in very heavy models, but then it must be disclosed prominently. Where the model relies on intentional circularity, iterative calculation must be enabled and the requirement stated, since the model returns errors on any machine where that setting is switched off.

column8: The overall structure (calculation flow, number of worksheets, level of detail) should be appropriate for the model's stated purpose.
column9: Structure is well-suited to the model's purpose: logical calculation flow, appropriate number of worksheets, and the right level of detail for the stated purpose.
column10: Structure is inappropriate (illogical flow, too many or too few sheets, mismatched detail level).
column11: Is the overall model structure appropriate for the model's purpose (e.g. consistent calculation flow, appropriate number of worksheets, sufficiently detailed)?
column12: The overall structure - calculation flow, number of worksheets, level of detail - is a primary determinant of model quality, and a logical structure is what makes a model auditable, maintainable, and understandable.

column8: Intermediate calculations must retain full precision; round only the final outputs presented to users. Display formatting (e.g., showing 0 decimals) is acceptable, as it does not change the underlying value. Rounding inside the model is legitimate only where the quantity is genuinely discrete (e.g., headcount, units sold, share counts) or where a contract or the case context specifies it.
column9: Intermediate calculations retain full precision; rounding is applied only to outputs, to genuinely discrete quantities, or where the case context requires it.
column10: Intermediate calculations are rounded without justification, compounding precision errors through the model.
column11: Do intermediate calculations retain full precision, with rounding applied only to outputs or where genuinely justified?
column12: Rounding intermediate calculations compounds precision errors through the model and is not standard practice: keep full precision internally and round only outputs. Display formatting (e.g., showing two decimal places) does not affect the underlying value and is always acceptable. Genuine exceptions exist - headcount, units, and share counts are discrete, and contractual terms may specify rounding - and these should be applied deliberately and labeled, not left implicit.

column8: Final outputs should be rounded to a sensible precision that communicates the appropriate level of certainty. (Rounding precision might be dictated for the questions)
column9: Final outputs are rounded to a sensible, readable precision.
column10: Final outputs show full, false precision.
column11: Are final outputs rounded?
column12: Outputs presented to users should be rounded to a sensible precision so they are readable and communicate the appropriate level of certainty.

column8: Rounding conventions should be documented in visible proximity to the rounded figure (e.g., '$ in millions, rounded to nearest $0.1m').
column9: Rounding conventions are documented next to the rounded figures.
column10: Rounding is undocumented or stated far from the figures.
column11: Is the rounding of outputs documented clearly and in visible proximity to the rounded figure?
column12: Documenting rounding conventions near the rounded figures (e.g., '$ in millions, rounded') prevents readers from assuming false precision and is standard practice in client-facing deliverables.

column8: The model should include all essential components: cover page, table of contents, summary/dashboard, assumptions, scenarios (where applicable), calculation sheets, financial statements (where applicable), error-check sheet, and output data. Components should be scaled to the model's size and purpose; in a small model several may reasonably sit on fewer sheets, provided each function remains clearly delineated.
column9: All essential components are present: cover, table of contents, summary, assumptions, scenarios (if applicable), calculations, statements (if applicable), error-check sheet, and outputs - or, in a small model, these functions are clearly delineated across fewer sheets.
column10: One or more essential components are missing.
column11: Does the model include all essential components appropriate to its size and purpose (cover page, table of contents, summary, assumptions, scenarios, calculations, financial statements, error checks, and outputs)?
column12: Every model needs its core building blocks: a cover page for context, a table of contents for navigation, an assumptions sheet for inputs, calculation sheets, scenarios where the analysis depends on uncertain drivers, financial statements where the model produces them, an error-check sheet, and an output summary for the audience. Missing components undermine completeness. In a small model several of these functions may reasonably share a sheet, provided each remains clearly delineated and labeled.

column8: The cover sheet should be the first tab, setting context and orienting the user on opening - typically stating the model's title, purpose, owner, version, and date.
column9: The cover sheet is the first tab and states the model's title, purpose, owner, version, and date.
column10: The cover sheet is missing, is not the first tab, or omits basic identifying information.
column11: Is the cover sheet the first tab of the workbook?
column12: A cover sheet as the first tab sets the context, describes the model's purpose, and orients the user immediately upon opening the file. It is the industry-standard first touchpoint.
column14: Applies: cases implying a multi-sheet workbook, where a dedicated cover tab is the natural entry point and its position in the tab order is a real design choice. N/A: cases implying a genuinely single-sheet deliverable, where a titled header block at the top of that sheet does the same job and 'first tab' has no meaning. How to tell from the starting file: ask whether the case warrants separate input, calculation and output sheets - several schedules, linked statements, or a summary to present. If yes, apply. Note: this item governs placement only. The requirement that the model carry cover and title information somewhere - name, purpose, owner, version, date - is a separate check that stays in force for every model, so a build with no cover information anywhere is still penalized there even where this item is marked N/A.

column8: Within calculation tabs, the timeline should run horizontally as standard - periods across columns, line items down rows - and be applied consistently. Period columns should align across tabs, so that a given column refers to the same period everywhere in the workbook (given no time period length shift). A vertical timeline (periods down rows) is acceptable where the tab's content justifies it, but should not be the default.
column9: Timeline runs horizontally on all calculation tabs, with periods occupying identical columns across the workbook. Where a vertical orientation is used, it is justified by the content - typically a register or data table where each record needs several attribute columns (ID, currency, rate, source, flags) visible simultaneously, and the number of periods is small enough to scan without excessive scrolling. The choice is consistent within each tab, and the reason for any deviation is evident from the tab itself.
column10: Orientation is mixed within a single tab, or varies across tabs with no rationale. Period columns are misaligned between tabs (e.g. Jan-24 sits in column H on one sheet and column K on another), creating link risk. A vertical timeline is used by default, forcing constant vertical scrolling to compare periods and breaking the copy-right formula convention. Alternatively, a horizontal timeline is forced onto a record-based table, pushing essential attribute columns off-screen.
column11: Does the model use a consistent timeline orientation - horizontal as standard, with period columns aligned across tabs - and where a vertical orientation appears, is it justified by that tab's content?
column12: A horizontal timeline - periods across columns, line items down rows - is the convention every reviewer expects, and it is what makes copying a formula rightwards across the timeline safe and predictable. Period columns should occupy the same columns on every tab, so a cross-sheet link cannot silently pick up the wrong period. A vertical timeline is acceptable where the tab's content justifies it - typically a register or data table where each record needs several attribute columns visible at once - but it should never be the default, and the reason should be evident from the tab itself.
column14: Applies: any case that lays periods out across the model - forecasts, schedules, budgets, cash-flow, coupon or amortiztion schedules, and daily, monthly, quarterly or annual builds. N/A: cases with no time dimension - snapshot valuations, single-period calculations, static registers or comparable sets with no periodicity. How to tell from the starting file: is there a forecast horizon, a schedule, or a period-based deliverable? Note that a comparables table with a 'fiscal period' column per company is NOT a timeline - each row is a different entity's reporting date, not a period axis - so that case is N/A. Where applicable: the test covers both the choice of orientation (horizontal as standard) and its consistency across tabs, including whether a given column refers to the same period on every sheet.

column8: Columns and rows containing the same type of information should be aligned vertically across the sheet, with a logical flow in the alignment of different calculations.
column9: Same-type columns and rows are aligned vertically, and the arrangement of different calculations follows a logical flow.
column10: Similar information is misaligned vertically; the arrangement of calculations lacks a logical flow.
column11: Are columns and rows of the same type of information aligned vertically with a logical flow?
column12: Vertical alignment of same-type data (e.g., all period columns at the same position, all unit columns in the same place) supports efficient scanning and cross-sheet formula construction. A logical flow makes the model intuitive to navigate.

column8: Subtitles, categories, and calculation names should be aligned with their respective values so the reader can clearly associate each label with the data it describes.
column9: Subtitles, categories, and calculation names are aligned with their respective values; associations are immediately clear.
column10: Labels are offset from or misaligned with their respective values, making it unclear which label belongs to which data.
column11: Are subtitles, categories, and calculation names aligned with their respective values?
column12: Misaligned labels force the reader to guess which label belongs to which row or column of data - a common source of misinterpretation. Clear label-to-value alignment is essential for readability and auditability.

column8: Beyond being merely acceptable, the structure should be the best fit given the model's specific requirements, audience, and foreseeable future uses. This item fails only where a clearly better alternative exists and can be articulated.
column9: The structure is well-justified as the best choice for the model's requirements, audience, and foreseeable future uses.
column10: A clearly better structure exists for the model's requirements, audience, or foreseeable uses, and the chosen structure creates avoidable friction.
column11: Is the chosen structure the best fit given the model's requirements, audience, and foreseeable uses?
column12: This item goes one step beyond basic appropriateness: even a workable structure may not be the best available given the model's specific requirements, audience, and foreseeable future uses. It should be judged only where a clearly better alternative can be identified and articulated, so that a sound structure is not penalized for failing to be theoretically perfect.

column8: The structure (calculation architecture) should reflect whether the model is for one-time deal evaluation or ongoing planning, as these require different data-refresh cadence, flexibility, and reporting depth.
column9: Structure (calculation architecture) matches the model's deal-evaluation or ongoing-planning purpose.
column10: Structure does not match the deal-vs-planning intent.
column11: Does the structure match whether the model is for one-time deal evaluation or for ongoing planning?
column12: A model built for one-time deal evaluation has different structural requirements than one designed for ongoing planning: refresh cadence, the flexibility built into the timeline, and the depth of reporting all differ. This item assesses the structure itself; whether the build is flexible enough for later reuse is assessed separately under flexibility.
column14: Applies: cases the brief frames either as a transaction or deal appraisal (LBO, M&A, project or investment appraisal, a valuation supporting a one-off decision, the pricing of an instrument for a buy-or-not decision) or as an ongoing planning tool (budget, forecast, operating plan, FP&A model, liquidity monitoring) - the structure should visibly reflect which. N/A: cases that are neither - a technical schedule, a reporting or compliance calculation, a pricing, costing or capacity-sizing tool with no deal or planning frame. How to tell from the starting file: read the task header and the question set. 'FP&A task ... build an integrated 3-statement model / working capital model' is a planning frame; 'valuation task ... value the company' is a deal frame. Mark N/A only where neither fits.

column8: The model must handle the entity's real fiscal calendar, including non-calendar year-ends (e.g., July-June). Where the case context specifies no fiscal calendar, a calendar-year assumption is acceptable provided it is stated.
column9: The model correctly reflects the entity's fiscal year, including non-calendar year-ends - or no fiscal calendar is specified and the assumption used is stated.
column10: The model assumes a calendar year where the case context specifies a different fiscal year-end, or the assumption is left unstated.
column11: Does the model handle the entity's real fiscal year, including non-calendar year-ends?
column12: Many companies have non-calendar fiscal years (e.g., July-June). The model must handle the real fiscal calendar to avoid systematic mismatches with reported financials and misdated periods. Where the case context specifies no fiscal calendar, a calendar-year assumption is acceptable provided it is stated explicitly.
column14: Applies: any case tied to a real entity's reporting calendar, or where the brief states a year-end, mentions interim reporting, mixes entities with different fiscal year-ends that must be aligned, or requires the model to tie back to reported financials. N/A in two situations: abstract models running on generic 'Year 1 ... Year n' periods with no entity calendar and no reporting tie; AND cases that supply already-prepared figures with an explicit instruction to use them as given - there the brief switches the calendarization question off, so do not penalize the model for leaving differing period ends unaligned. How to tell from the starting file: look for year-end dates, fiscal period columns or a stated calendar in the pack, then check whether the brief asks for any adjustment. A stated start date of 1 January with annual periods and no other calendar reference is a calendar-year assumption, which the model must state but which does not by itself make this item demanding.

column8: Stub periods (partial periods at the start or end of a forecast) must be calculated correctly using a day-count convention (actual/365, actual/360, 30/360) appropriate to the model's purpose, the case context/instructions, and the jurisdiction. A model whose periods are all full periods satisfies this item by default.
column9: Stub periods are calculated correctly with an appropriate day-count convention - or the model contains no stub periods.
column10: Stub periods arise but are mishandled or ignored.
column11: Are stub periods/partial years handled correctly (or does the model contain none)?
column12: Stub periods (partial periods at the beginning or end of a forecast) are a common source of error and are easy to overlook, because the model still computes cleanly under a full-period assumption. They must be calculated using a day-count convention appropriate to the jurisdiction and instrument type so that valuations and totals are accurate. Where every period is a full period, the item is satisfied by default.
column14: Applies: wherever the case creates a partial period - a valuation, as-of or start date falling mid-period, a transaction closing mid-period, an asset placed in service or a building ready mid-month, debt drawn or repaid intra-period, an irregular first or last coupon, a forecast starting or ending off the period boundary, or a mid-year or mid-month discounting convention. N/A: cases whose periods are all full and aligned to the model's period grid, with no partial period anywhere. How to tell from the starting file: test every date on the assumptions tab against the period grid the brief implies - the grid decides. A 1 July start is a stub on an annual model but a full period on a monthly one; an issuance date a few weeks before the first coupon creates a stub on any grid. Where the brief names a day-count convention (actual/365, actual/360, 30/360, Canadian compound), a stub is almost certainly in scope.

column8: Cover, inputs, calculations, analyses, and outputs should each sit on separate sheets with no function mixing on a single sheet (unless there is a clear structural reason).
column9: Each function sits on its own sheet with no mixing (unless there is a clear structural reason).
column10: Functions are mixed on the same sheet (e.g., inputs and calculations together).
column11: Are all worksheets separated by function? (cover, inputs, calculations, analyses, outputs/summaries on separate sheets, no mixing on one sheet)
column12: Separation by function (cover, inputs, calculations, outputs on separate sheets) is a core modeling principle that makes the model auditable, reduces error risk, and allows changes in one area without impacting the whole model.
column14: Applies: any case large enough to warrant more than one sheet - where assumptions, calculations, statements, analyses and outputs each carry enough content to stand alone. N/A: a genuinely small case deliberately built on one sheet, provided cover, inputs, calculations and outputs sit in clearly delineated, labeled blocks. How to tell from the starting file: if the case pack itself separates instructions, assumptions, data and questions across tabs, the submitted build should be at least as separated - apply. Reserve N/A for the smallest cases: one supplied table, one calculation, one answer.
